args.text: [lane-plover] Three risks of caching DNS (Domain Name System) answers for too long: (1) Stale answers: users are sent to an old address after a server moves or fails, so the service looks down. (2) Slow recovery: a fix or failover change takes a long time to reach everyone, because old answers linger. (3) Lingering bad data: if a wrong or poisoned answer is cached, it keeps being served until it expires.

[lane-plover] Idempotent retries matter because a request that is repeated after a timeout or failure may or may not have worked the first time, and an idempotent one gives the same result however many times it runs. This stops harmful side effects, such as charging a customer twice, and lets systems retry safely without guessing.

[lane-plover] Two trade-offs of UUIDv7 (Universally Unique Identifier, version 7) as a primary key: (1) Good for storage order, since ids rise with time and keep database indexes tidy, but they reveal roughly when a row was created, which may leak information. (2) They are 16 bytes, larger than a standard 4 or 8 byte integer, so indexes and joins use more space and can be slightly slower.

[lane-plover] A write-ahead log is a record where a database writes each change down before applying it to the main data files. If the system crashes, it can replay this record to recover completed changes and undo unfinished ones, so no data is lost or left half-written.

[lane-plover] Two reasons to pin a client version in a benchmark: (1) Fair comparison: if the client changes between runs, a speed difference might come from the client rather than the system being tested. (2) Repeatability: others can rerun the same setup later and get comparable results, without surprise changes from automatic updates.

[lane-plover] Backpressure is a way for a busy queue to signal producers to slow down, pause or stop sending work when consumers cannot keep up. This keeps the queue from growing without limit and running out of memory, so the system stays stable instead of failing under load.

[lane-plover] Two ways a cron job can run twice: (1) The same schedule is installed on two servers, for example after scaling out or a failover copy. (2) A slow run is still going when the next scheduled run starts, so the two overlap. One guard: take a lock before starting, such as a lock file or database lock, and exit at once if another run already holds it.

[lane-plover] A tombstone is a marker stored in place of a deleted item in a replicated store. It tells every copy that the item was removed, so a replica that missed the delete does not bring the old value back. Tombstones are cleaned up only after a set period, long enough for all copies to see them. That period is unknown here, as it depends on the system's settings.

[lane-plover] Two signs that a test is flaky rather than failing: (1) It passes and fails on the same code, with no change between runs. (2) The failure depends on timing, order or environment, such as passing alone but failing alongside other tests, or failing only on a busy machine.

[lane-plover] A lease-based lock gives a client the lock for a set time, and everyone relies on clocks to decide when that time is up. With clock skew (clocks that disagree), a client with a slow clock may think it still holds the lock after the lock service has given it to someone else. Two clients then act as owner at once, which breaks the lock's promise.

[lane-plover] Two costs of very long feature branches: (1) Painful merges, because the main branch keeps changing and the two drift apart, so conflicts pile up and are harder to settle correctly. (2) Late feedback, because reviewers and tests see a huge change all at once, so problems are found late, reviews are shallow, and fixing them costs more.

[lane-plover] A canary release sends a new version to a small share of real users or servers first, while most keep the old version. It checks whether the new version behaves well in real conditions, such as error rates, speed and resource use, so a fault can be caught and rolled back before it reaches everyone.

[lane-plover] Two risks of keeping secrets in environment variables: (1) they can leak through crash reports, logs or debugging output that dump the whole environment; (2) child processes inherit them by default, and anyone with access to the machine's process details may be able to read them, so they reach more places than intended.

[lane-plover] Latency is the time a request takes to get a response. The p50 (50th percentile, or median) is the time that half of requests beat, so it shows the typical experience. The p99 (99th percentile) is the time that 99 in every 100 requests beat, so it shows the slow tail that a small share of users still meet. A healthy p50 can hide a poor p99.
